study.title: Psalm 68 God rises up to save, lead and reign
study.overview: This psalm is a great song of victory and worship. He begins with the supplication for God to act against enemies, passes through the remembrance of God's care in the exodus and in the wilderness, celebrates the divine provision to his people, and ends up calling all the nations to praise the Lord. Throughout the poem, God appears as a victorious warrior, careful shepherd, enthroned king and source of strength for his people. The Protestant evangelical reading here recognizes a movement of exaltation of God that, in the notes received, is often linked to his performance in favor of Israel and, in Christian interpretation, also points to the reign of God that reaches the nations.

outline.title: Clamor that God rises and justice be celebrated
outline.explanation: The first verses ask God to manifest, scatter the enemies and cause the wicked to perish, while the righteous rejoice. The text also presents the character of God as the protector of the orphans and widows, the deliverer of the prisoners and the one who gives abode to the lonely.

outline.title: God leads his people from the desert to the chosen dwelling
outline.explanation: The second part recalls God's march with his people in the wilderness, his tremendous presence at Sinai and his provision for the tired inheritance. Then the psalm describes God's victory over kings and the arrival of his chosen mountain as a place of permanent dwelling.

outline.title: Salvation, judgment and expansion of God's recognition
outline.explanation: Here the psalm claims that God carries his people day after day and delivers from death. At the same time, he announces judgment on the enemies and submission of peoples and kings, including figures from Egypt and Kusket, showing that honor to God widens beyond Israel.

outline.title: Universal Invitation to the Final Praise and Godship
outline.explanation: The conclusion summons the kingdoms of the earth to sing to the Lord, affirms their sovereignty over the heavens and ends with a confession: the God of Israel is the one who gives strength and power to the people. The psalm closes with blessing and reverence.

study.context: The notes provided suggest that the psalm celebrates the action of God since the departure of Egypt, the conduction through the desert and the entrance into the promised land, with language linked to the divine march and the installation of his kingdom. Matthew Henry understands that the psalm was probably written when the ark was taken to Zion, and that this led the psalmist to speak, by prophetic inspiration, of greater things connected with the Messiah and his kingdom. This reading is interpretative, not an explicit information from the biblical text itself.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that God is not passive: he rises up, acts in history and defeats evil. His holiness appears both in the judgment on the wicked and in compassion for the vulnerable. He is the God of providence, who sustains the people on the way, and the God of presence, who dwells among his people. The strength of the psalm is in uniting victory and care, power and mercy. The notes also highlight a broader horizon: when God manifests his majesty, he strengthens his people and draws the nations to praise. In Christian reading, many see here an anticipation of God's universal reign and the exaltation of his anointed, but this should be treated as theological interpretation, not as a direct and unequivocal affirmation of the psalm.

scholarViews.insight: The initial verses are a prayer that God may rise up and spread his enemies, as he did when Israel entered the promised land; the image of the smoke and the wax underscores the fragility of the wicked before God.
The psalmist recalls that God guided Israel through the desert; the remembrance of past mercies must renew gratitude for divine care on the way.
The closure of the psalm declares that the God who dwells in his holy places is fearful and at the same time is the one who gives strength and power to his people.

questions: How does this psalm correct the idea that God is far from human conflicts?
How can the remembrance of God's care in the past strengthen faith today?
How does the invitation to nations to praise God challenge a faith restricted only to the religious group itself?
study.practice: Read this psalm as a prayer and not just as a poem. Confess before God his areas of fear, injustice and exhaustion, and ask him to stand up for what is just. Then practice the spiritual memory: write down concrete forms by which God has already sustained you and your community. Finally, a worship and mission: Praise God with sincerity and pray that people from other places and nations will also recognize their sovereignty.
study.uncertainty: Some verses are difficult to interpret, and the notes provided recognize this. It is not possible to affirm with certainty, only on the basis of this material, the exact occasion of the composition of the psalm. Nor should any reading that directly and exclusively identify specific messianic or historical references; this remains a probable theological interpretation, supported by the notes, but not demonstrated in an absolute way by the text.
